sentence: A custom kept everywhere in the Church may fairly be presumed apostolic, even where no apostle's own writing says so.

records.means: Cyprian would call a rite the apostles' own only if it was written; Augustine would too if the whole Church kept it in all lands.
records.text: We do not agree among ourselves on one test for whether a practice of ours truly came from the apostles. Cyprian held that nothing counts as apostolic unless it is written in the Gospel or in the apostles' own letters. Custom alone, however old, is not enough. Custom without truth, he said, is only the old age of error. Augustine took up a related question about 150 years later. He used a different test. A custom kept everywhere in the Church may fairly be presumed apostolic, even where no apostle's own writing says so. We give you both tests, because both are ours. In this very dispute, Augustine used his test on one practice. He held that not baptizing again someone baptized among heretics came down from the apostles. Elsewhere he said the same of baptizing infants. Neither test traces the road back, or the teaching before the water, to the apostles.

He asked Lucian to grant his wish and grieve with him over her death, a death of the spirit, for in that time of ruin she had fallen away from Christ. She was not dead. What Celerinus grieved was a death he believed had happened to her soul -- which is why the letter carries a request. He asked Lucian to intervene, for her and for two other women, Numeria and Candida, whom Lucian also knew. He made the case for them: they had repented, and there were works to point to. sentence: We tell you it was real, in one of our own, and that it was not the end of his story.
